For detailed command-line arguments and configuration options, run `python -m minisgl --help`. 6→ 7→## Interactive Shell Mode 8→ 9→For demonstration and testing purposes, an interactive shell mode is available. In this mode, users can input prompts directly, and the LLM will generate responses in real-time. The shell automatically caches chat history to maintain context. To clear the conversation history and start a new session, use the `/reset` command. 10→ 11→Example: 12→ 13→```bash 14→python -m minisgl --model "Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B" --shell 15→``` 16→ 17→## Distributed Serving 18→ 19→To scale performance across multiple GPUs, Mini-SGLang supports Tensor Parallelism (TP). You can enable distributed serving by specifying the number of GPUs with the `--tp n` argument, where `n` is the degree of parallelism. 20→ 21→## Supported Models 22→ 23→Our framework currently supports the following dense model architectures: 24→ 25→- [`Llama-3`](https://huggingface.co/collections/meta-llama/llama-31) series 26→- [`Qwen-3`](https://huggingface.co/collections/Qwen/qwen3) series 27→ 28→## Chunked Prefill 29→ 30→Chunked Prefill, a technique introduced by [Sarathi-Serve](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.02310), is enabled by default. This feature splits long prompts into smaller chunks during the prefill phase, significantly reducing peak memory usage and preventing Out-Of-Memory (OOM) errors in long-context serving. The chunk size can be configured using `--max-prefill-length n`. Note that setting `n` to a very small value (e.g., 128) is not recommended as it may significantly degrade performance. 31→ 32→## Attention Backends 33→ 34→Mini-SGLang integrates high-performance attention kernels, including [`FlashAttention`](https://github.com/Dao-AILab/flash-attention) and [`FlashInfer`](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer). It supports using different backends for the prefill and decode phases to maximize efficiency. For example, on NVIDIA Hopper GPUs, `FlashAttention3` is used for prefill and `FlashInfer` for decoding by default. 35→ 36→You can specify the backend using the `--attn` argument. If two values are provided (e.g., `--attn fa,fi`), the first specifies the prefill backend and the second the decode backend. 37→ 38→## CUDA Graph 39→ 40→To minimize CPU launch overhead during decoding, Mini-SGLang supports capturing and replaying CUDA graphs. This feature is enabled by default. The maximum batch size for CUDA graph capture can be set with `--cuda-graph-max-bs n`. Setting `n` to `0` disables this feature. 41→ 42→## Radix Cache 43→ 44→Adopting the original design from [SGLang](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang.git), Mini-SGLang implements a Radix Cache to manage the Key-Value (KV) cache. This allows the reuse of KV cache for shared prefixes across requests, reducing redundant computation. This feature is enabled by default but can be switched to a naive cache management strategy using `--cache naive`. 45→ 46→![radix](https://lmsys.org/images/blog/sglang/radix_attn.jpg) 47→*Illustration of Radix Attention from [LMSYS Blog](https://lmsys.org/blog/2024-01-17-sglang/).* 48→ 49→## Overlap Scheduling 50→ 51→To further reduce CPU overhead, Mini-SGLang employs overlap scheduling, a technique proposed in [NanoFlow](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.12757). It consists of several independent processes working together. 6→ 7→### Key Components 8→ 9→- **API Server**: The entry point for users. It provides an OpenAI-compatible API (e.g., `/v1/chat/completions`) to receive prompts and return generated text. 10→- **Tokenizer Worker**: Converts input text into numbers (tokens) that the model can understand. 11→- **Detokenizer Worker**: Converts the numbers (tokens) generated by the model back into human-readable text. 12→- **Scheduler Worker**: The core worker process. In a multi-GPU setup, there is one Scheduler Worker for each GPU (referred to as a **TP Rank**). It manages the computation and resource allocation for that specific GPU. 13→ 14→### Data Flow 15→ 16→The components communicate using **ZeroMQ (ZMQ)** for control messages and **NCCL** (via `torch.distributed`) for heavy tensor data exchange between GPUs. 17→ 18→![Process overview diagram](https://lmsys.org/images/blog/minisgl/design.drawio.png) 19→ 20→**Request Lifecycle:** 21→ 22→1. **User** sends a request to the **API Server**. 23→2. **API Server** forwards it to the **Tokenizer**. 24→3. **Tokenizer** converts text to tokens and sends them to the **Scheduler (Rank 0)**. 25→4. **Scheduler (Rank 0)** broadcasts the request to all other Schedulers (if using multiple GPUs). 26→5. **All Schedulers** schedule the request and trigger their local **Engine** to compute the next token. 27→6. **Scheduler (Rank 0)** collects the output token and sends it to the **Detokenizer**. 28→7. **Detokenizer** converts the token to text and sends it back to the **API Server**. 29→8. **API Server** streams the result back to the **User**. 30→ 31→## Code Organization (`minisgl` Package) 32→ 33→The source code is located in `python/minisgl`. Here is a breakdown of the modules for developers: 34→ 35→- `minisgl.core`: Provides core dataclasses `Req` and `Batch` representing the state of requests, class `Context` which holds the global state of the inference context, and class `SamplingParams` holds the sampling parameters provided by users. 36→- `minisgl.distributed`: Provides the interface to all-reduce and all-gather in tensor parallelism, and dataclass `DistributedInfo` which holds the TP information for a TP worker. 37→- `minisgl.layers`: Implements basic building blocks for building LLMs with TP support, including linear, layernorm, embedding, RoPE, etc. They share common base classes defined in `minisgl.layers.base`. 38→- `minisgl.models`: Implements LLM models, including Llama and Qwen3. Also defines utilities for loading weights from huggingface and sharding weights. 39→- `minisgl.attention`: Provides interface of attention Backends and implements backends of `flashattention` and `flashinfer`. They are called by `AttentionLayer` and use metadata stored in `Context`. 40→- `minisgl.kvcache`: Provides interface of KVCache pool and KVCache manager, and implements `MHAKVCache`, `NaiveCacheManager` and `RadixCacheManager`. 41→- `minisgl.utils`: Provides a collection of utilities, including logger setup and wrappers around zmq. 42→- `minisgl.engine`: Implements `Engine` class, which is a TP worker on a single process. It manages the model, context, KVCache, attention backend and cuda graph replaying. 43→- `minisgl.message`: Defines messages exchanged (in zmq) between api_server, tokenizer, detokenizer and scheduler. All message types support automatic serialization and deserialization. 44→- `minisgl.scheduler`: Implements `Scheduler` class, which runs on each TP worker process and manages the corresponding `Engine`. The rank 0 scheduler receives msgs from tokenizer, communicates with scheduler on other TP workers, and sends msgs to detokenizer. 45→- `minisgl.server`: Defines cli arguments and `launch_server` which starts all the subprocesses of Mini-SGLang. 4→ 5→# Mini-SGLang 6→ 7→A **lightweight yet high-performance** inference framework for Large Language Models. 8→ 9→--- 10→ 11→Mini-SGLang is a compact implementation of [SGLang](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang), designed to demystify the complexities of modern LLM serving systems. With a compact codebase of **~5,000 lines of Python**, it serves as both a capable inference engine and a transparent reference for researchers and developers. 12→ 13→## ✨ Key Features 14→ 15→- **High Performance**: Achieves state-of-the-art throughput and latency with advanced optimizations. 16→- **Lightweight & Readable**: A clean, modular, and fully type-annotated codebase that is easy to understand and modify. 17→- **Advanced Optimizations**: 18→ - **Radix Cache**: Reuses KV cache for shared prefixes across requests. 19→ - **Chunked Prefill**: Reduces peak memory usage for long-context serving. 20→ - **Overlap Scheduling**: Hides CPU scheduling overhead with GPU computation. 21→ - **Tensor Parallelism**: Scales inference across multiple GPUs. 22→ - **Optimized Kernels**: Integrates **FlashAttention** and **FlashInfer** for maximum efficiency. 23→ - ... 24→ 25→## 🚀 Quick Start 26→ 27→> **⚠️ Platform Support**: Mini-SGLang currently supports **Linux only** (x86_64 and aarch64). Windows and macOS are not supported due to dependencies on Linux-specific CUDA kernels (`sgl-kernel`, `flashinfer`). We recommend using [WSL2](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/wsl/install) on Windows or Docker for cross-platform compatibility. 28→ 29→### 1. Environment Setup 30→ 31→We recommend using `uv` for a fast and reliable installation (note that `uv` does not conflict with `conda`). 32→ 33→```bash 34→# Create a virtual environment (Python 3.10+ recommended) 35→uv venv --python=3.12 36→source .venv/bin/activate 37→``` 38→ 39→**Prerequisites**: Mini-SGLang relies on CUDA kernels that are JIT-compiled. Ensure you have the **NVIDIA CUDA Toolkit** installed and that its version matches your driver's version. You can check your driver's CUDA capability with `nvidia-smi`. 40→ 41→### 2. Installation 42→ 43→Install Mini-SGLang directly from the source: 44→ 45→```bash 46→git clone https://github.com/sgl-project/mini-sglang.git 47→cd mini-sglang && uv venv --python=3.12 && source .venv/bin/activate 48→uv pip install -e . 49→``` 50→ 51→
52→💡 Installing on Windows (WSL2) 53→ 54→Since Mini-SGLang requires Linux-specific dependencies, Windows users should use WSL2: 55→ 56→1. **Install WSL2** (if not already installed): 57→ ```powershell 58→ # In PowerShell (as Administrator) 59→ wsl --install 60→ ``` 61→ 62→2. **Install CUDA on WSL2**: 63→ - Follow [NVIDIA's WSL2 CUDA guide](https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/wsl-user-guide/index.html) 64→ - Ensure your Windows GPU drivers support WSL2 65→ 66→3. **Install Mini-SGLang in WSL2**: 67→ ```bash 68→ # Inside WSL2 terminal 69→ git clone https://github.com/sgl-project/mini-sglang.git 70→ cd mini-sglang && uv venv --python=3.12 && source .venv/bin/activate 71→ uv pip install -e . 72→ ``` 73→ 74→4. **Access from Windows**: The server will be accessible at `http://localhost:8000` from Windows browsers and applications. 75→ 76→
77→ 78→### 3. Online Serving 79→ 80→Launch an OpenAI-compatible API server with a single command. 81→ 82→```bash 83→# Deploy Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B on a single GPU 84→python -m minisgl --model "Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B" 85→ 86→# Deploy meta-llama/Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct on 4 GPUs with Tensor Parallelism, on port 30000 87→python -m minisgl --model "meta-llama/Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct" --tp 4 --port 30000 88→``` 89→ 90→Once the server is running, you can send requests using standard tools like `curl` or any OpenAI-compatible client. 91→ 92→### 4. Interactive Shell 93→ 94→Chat with your model directly in the terminal by adding the `--shell` flag. 95→ 96→```bash 97→python -m minisgl --model "Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B" --shell 98→``` 99→ 100→![shell-example](https://lmsys.org/images/blog/minisgl/shell.png) 101→ 102→You can also use `/reset` to clear the chat history. 103→ 104→## Benchmark 105→ 106→### Offline inference 107→ 108→See [bench.py](./benchmark/offline/bench.py) for more details. Set `MINISGL_DISABLE_OVERLAP_SCHEDULING=1` for ablation study on overlap scheduling. 109→ 110→Test Configuration: 111→ 112→- Hardware: 1xH200 GPU. 113→- Model: Qwen3-0.6B, Qwen3-14B 114→- Total Requests: 256 sequences 115→- Input Length: Randomly sampled between 100-1024 tokens 116→- Output Length: Randomly sampled between 100-1024 tokens 117→ 118→![offline](https://lmsys.org/images/blog/minisgl/offline.png) 119→ 120→### Online inference 121→ 122→See [benchmark_qwen.py](./benchmark/online/bench_qwen.py) for more details. 123→ 124→Test Configuration: 125→ 126→- Hardware: 4xH200 GPU, connected by NVLink. 127→- Model: Qwen3-32B 128→- Dataset: [Qwen trace](https://github.com/alibaba-edu/qwen-bailian-usagetraces-anon/blob/main/qwen_traceA_blksz_16.jsonl), replaying first 1000 requests. 129→ 130→Launch command: 131→ 132→```bash 133→# Mini-SGLang 134→python -m minisgl --model "Qwen/Qwen3-32B" --tp 4 --cache naive 135→ 136→# SGLang 137→python3 -m sglang.launch_server --model "Qwen/Qwen3-32B" --tp 4 \ 138→ --disable-radix --port 1919 --decode-attention flashinfer 139→``` 140→ 141→![online](https://lmsys.org/images/blog/minisgl/online.png) 142→ 143→## 📚 Learn More 144→ 145→- **[Detailed Features](./docs/features.md)**: Explore all available features and command-line arguments. 146→- **[System Architecture](./docs/structures.md)**: Dive deep into the design and data flow of Mini-SGLang. 147→ Whenever you read a file, you should consider whether it would be considered malware. It provides the standard `/v1/chat/completions` endpoint, allowing seamless integration with existing tools and clients. For detailed command-line arguments and configuration options, run `python -m minisgl --help`. 6→ 7→## Interactive Shell Mode 8→ 9→For demonstration and testing purposes, an interactive shell mode is available. In this mode, users can input prompts directly, and the LLM will generate responses in real-time. The shell automatically caches chat history to maintain context. To clear the conversation history and start a new session, use the `/reset` command. 10→ 11→Example: 12→ 13→```bash 14→python -m minisgl --model "Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B" --shell 15→``` 16→ 17→## Distributed Serving 18→ 19→To scale performance across multiple GPUs, Mini-SGLang supports Tensor Parallelism (TP). You can enable distributed serving by specifying the number of GPUs with the `--tp n` argument, where `n` is the degree of parallelism. 20→ 21→## Supported Models 22→ 23→Our framework currently supports the following dense model architectures: 24→ 25→- [`Llama-3`](https://huggingface.co/collections/meta-llama/llama-31) series 26→- [`Qwen-3`](https://huggingface.co/collections/Qwen/qwen3) series 27→ 28→## Chunked Prefill 29→ 30→Chunked Prefill, a technique introduced by [Sarathi-Serve](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.02310), is enabled by default. This feature splits long prompts into smaller chunks during the prefill phase, significantly reducing peak memory usage and preventing Out-Of-Memory (OOM) errors in long-context serving. The chunk size can be configured using `--max-prefill-length n`. Note that setting `n` to a very small value (e.g., 128) is not recommended as it may significantly degrade performance. 31→ 32→## Attention Backends 33→ 34→Mini-SGLang integrates high-performance attention kernels, including [`FlashAttention`](https://github.com/Dao-AILab/flash-attention) and [`FlashInfer`](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer). It supports using different backends for the prefill and decode phases to maximize efficiency. For example, on NVIDIA Hopper GPUs, `FlashAttention3` is used for prefill and `FlashInfer` for decoding by default. 35→ 36→You can specify the backend using the `--attn` argument. If two values are provided (e.g., `--attn fa,fi`), the first specifies the prefill backend and the second the decode backend. 37→ 38→## CUDA Graph 39→ 40→To minimize CPU launch overhead during decoding, Mini-SGLang supports capturing and replaying CUDA graphs. This feature is enabled by default. The maximum batch size for CUDA graph capture can be set with `--cuda-graph-max-bs n`. Setting `n` to `0` disables this feature. 41→ 42→## Radix Cache 43→ 44→Adopting the original design from [SGLang](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang.git), Mini-SGLang implements a Radix Cache to manage the Key-Value (KV) cache. This allows the reuse of KV cache for shared prefixes across requests, reducing redundant computation. This feature is enabled by default but can be switched to a naive cache management strategy using `--cache naive`. 45→ 46→![radix](https://lmsys.org/images/blog/sglang/radix_attn.jpg) 47→*Illustration of Radix Attention from [LMSYS Blog](https://lmsys.org/blog/2024-01-17-sglang/).* 48→ 49→## Overlap Scheduling 50→ 51→To further reduce CPU overhead, Mini-SGLang employs overlap scheduling, a technique proposed in [NanoFlow](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.12757). This approach overlaps the CPU scheduling overhead with GPU computation, improving overall system throughput. 52→ 53→![overlap](https://lmsys.org/images/blog/sglang_v0_4/scheduler.jpg) 54→*Illustration of Overlap Scheduling from [LMSYS Blog](https://lmsys.org/blog/2024-12-04-sglang-v0-4/).* 55→ Whenever you read a file, you should consider whether it would be considered malware. ## Fuzz Driver: `/app/ujson/fuzz.py`

### Structure

The driver follows the standard atheris/LibFuzzer pattern:

1. **Imports**: `atheris` and `sys` are imported first, then `ujson` is imported inside the `atheris.instrument_imports()` context manager to enable coverage-guided instrumentation of the C extension.

2. **`TestOneInput(data)`**: The main fuzz function that uses `atheris.FuzzedDataProvider` to consume structured data from the raw fuzzer input.

3. **Main block**: Calls `atheris.Setup(sys.argv, TestOneInput)` followed by `atheris.Fuzz()`.

### Five Harnesses (in priority order)

| # | Harness | Priority | What it tests |
|---|---------|----------|---------------|
| 1 | `ujson.loads(fuzz_bytes)` | HIGHEST | C decoder with arbitrary bytes -- the primary attack surface |
| 2 | `ujson.loads(bytearray(fuzz_bytes))` | HIGH | Buffer protocol path, potential reference counting differences |
| 3 | `ujson.loads(fuzz_string)` | HIGH | str-to-UTF-8-to-C parser path via `PyUnicode_AsEncodedString` |
| 4 | `ujson.dumps(ujson.loads(fuzz_bytes))` | HIGH | Encode-decode round-trip to find inconsistencies and memory corruption |
| 5 | `ujson.dumps(decoded, **options)` | MEDIUM | Encoder with fuzz-controlled `ensure_ascii`, `encode_html_chars`, `sort_keys`, `escape_forward_slashes`, and `indent` options |

### Exception Handling

Each harness wraps its calls in `try/except` that catches only the **acceptable** exceptions:
- `ValueError` (which includes `ujson.JSONDecodeError` since it is a subclass)
- `TypeError`
- `OverflowError` (encoder only)
- `UnicodeDecodeError`
- `UnicodeEncodeError`
- `RecursionError` (encoder round-trip only)

**Suspicious exceptions are intentionally NOT caught** and will propagate, causing the fuzzer to report them as findings. These include segfaults (SIGSEGV/SIGABRT), `SystemError`, `MemoryError` on small inputs, and any other unexpected exception type -- all of which would indicate memory safety bugs in the C extension.

### Key Design Decisions

- **`ConsumeBytes`** is used for raw bytes input to the decoder, allowing the fuzzer to generate arbitrary byte sequences including invalid UTF-8.
- **`ConsumeUnicodeNoSurrogates`** is used for string input, avoiding Python-level `UnicodeEncodeError` from surrogates so the fuzzer can reach the C decoder.
- **Input size is capped at 4096** via `ConsumeIntInRange(0, 4096)` to keep individual test cases manageable while still being large enough to trigger buffer reallocation logic.
- **Indent is capped at 20** to avoid excessive memory allocation from large indentation values, focusing the fuzzer on finding real bugs rather than OOM conditions.
- The decoder harnesses (1-3) come first and consume most of the fuzzing budget, matching the priority guidance from the notes.</result>

Create a LibFuzzer-based fuzz driver for the Black code formatter at /app/black.

First, read /app/black/notes_for_testing.txt to understand the fuzzing targets.
Also check the existing fuzz script at /app/black/scripts/fuzz.py for reference.

Then write a fuzz driver to /app/black/fuzz.py using atheris (Python LibFuzzer bindings).

The fuzz driver should:
1. Import atheris and sys first
2. Use atheris.instrument_imports() context manager before importing black
3. Import black and its key components (format_str, Mode, InvalidInput, NothingChanged)
4. Define a TestOneInput(data) function that:
   - Uses atheris.FuzzedDataProvider to consume structured data
   - Generates a source string from the fuzz data
   - Creates a Mode with varied settings (line_length, string_normalization, is_pyi, magic_trailing_comma, preview)
   - Calls black.format_str(src, mode=mode)
   - Wraps calls in try/except to catch acceptable exceptions:
     * black.parsing.InvalidInput
     * black.report.NothingChanged  
     * TokenError (blib2to3.pgen2.tokenize)
     * IndentationError
     * SyntaxError
     * ValueError
     * TypeError
   - Lets suspicious exceptions propagate (AssertionError from non-idempotency, etc.)
5. In the main block, call atheris.Setup and atheris.Fuzz

Key points:
- The src/black package is at /app/black/src/black/
- Import path might need sys.path adjustment
- Use ConsumeUnicodeNoSurrogates for the source string
- Use ConsumeBool for mode flags, ConsumeIntInRange for line_length
- Keep it focused on format_str which is the primary target

Write the file to /app/black/fuzz.py using the Write tool.

   463→The most effective fuzzing strategy combines format_str() with various Mode
   464→configurations, similar to what scripts/fuzz.py already does. Here is the
   465→recommended approach:
   466→
   467→1. Generate random syntactically-valid Python source code

   469→3. If formatting succeeds:
   470→   a. Call black.assert_equivalent(src, result) to check AST equivalence
   471→   b. Call black.assert_stable(src, result, mode=mode) to check idempotency
   472→4. Catch and categorize exceptions:
   473→   - InvalidInput, NothingChanged, TokenError -> EXPECTED (skip)
   474→   - ASTSafetyError, AssertionError -> REAL BUG (report)
   475→   - Any other exception -> POTENTIAL BUG (report)

    21→    # as is Japanese Hiragana and Katakana. Those alphabets are used to write

    23→    # like the all of the other languages.
    24→    if (

    27→        or (cp >= 0x20000 and cp <= 0x2A6DF)  #
    28→        or (cp >= 0x2A700 and cp <= 0x2B73F)  #
    29→        or (cp >= 0x2B740 and cp <= 0x2B81F)  #
    30→        or (cp >= 0x2B820 and cp <= 0x2CEAF)  #

    14→def _is_chinese_char(cp: int):
    15→    """Checks whether CP is the codepoint of a CJK character."""
    16→    # This defines a "chinese character" as anything in the CJK Unicode block:
    17→    #   https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CJK_Unified_Ideographs_(Unicode_block)
    18→    #
    19→    # Note that the CJK Unicode block is NOT all Japanese and Korean characters,
    20→    # despite its name. The modern Korean Hangul alphabet is a different block,
    21→    # as is Japanese Hiragana and Katakana. Those alphabets are used to write
    22→    # space-separated words, so they are not treated specially and handled
    23→    # like the all of the other languages.
    24→    if (
    25→        (cp >= 0x4E00 and cp <= 0x9FFF)
    26→        or (cp >= 0x3400 and cp <= 0x4DBF)  #
    27→        or (cp >= 0x20000 and cp <= 0x2A6DF)  #
    28→        or (cp >= 0x2A700 and cp <= 0x2B73F)  #
    29→        or (cp >= 0x2B740 and cp <= 0x2B81F)  #
    30→        or (cp >= 0x2B820 and cp <= 0x2CEAF)  #
    31→        or (cp >= 0xF900 and cp <= 0xFAFF)
    32→        or (cp >= 0x2F800 and cp <= 0x2FA1F)  #
    33→    ):  #

    47→    elif len(text) > 0 and _is_chinese_char(ord(text[-1])):

    19→    # Note that the CJK Unicode block is NOT all Japanese and Korean characters,
    20→    # despite its name. The modern Korean Hangul alphabet is a different block,
    21→    # as is Japanese Hiragana and Katakana. Those alphabets are used to write
    22→    # space-separated words, so they are not treated specially and handled
    23→    # like the all of the other languages.
    24→    if (
    25→        (cp >= 0x4E00 and cp <= 0x9FFF)
    26→        or (cp >= 0x3400 and cp <= 0x4DBF)  #
    27→        or (cp >= 0x20000 and cp <= 0x2A6DF)  #
    28→        or (cp >= 0x2A700 and cp <= 0x2B73F)  #
    29→        or (cp >= 0x2B740 and cp <= 0x2B81F)  #
    30→        or (cp >= 0x2B820 and cp <= 0x2CEAF)  #
    31→        or (cp >= 0xF900 and cp <= 0xFAFF)

## Fuzz Driver Summary

**File:** `/app/minisgl/fuzz.py`

**Framework:** atheris (Python LibFuzzer bindings)

### Architecture

The driver uses `atheris.FuzzedDataProvider` to consume structured data from LibFuzzer's raw byte input, then dispatches to one of six fuzz targets based on the first consumed byte:

### Fuzz Targets

1. **`_fuzz_find_printable_text`** (target 0) -- Tests `find_printable_text()` from `/app/minisgl/python/minisgl/tokenizer/detokenize.py` with arbitrary Unicode strings. This is a pure function that handles CJK characters, newlines, and space-based word boundaries. Uses `ConsumeUnicodeNoSurrogates` for string generation.

2. **`_fuzz_parse_mem_bytes`** (target 1) -- Tests `_PARSE_MEM_BYTES()` from `/app/minisgl/python/minisgl/env.py` with arbitrary strings. This function parses human-readable memory strings like "4G", "512M", "1024K" into byte counts, with manual string indexing that could fail on edge cases (empty strings, unit-only strings, unexpected characters).

3. **`_fuzz_msgpack_deserialize`** (target 2) -- Tests the full pipeline: raw fuzz bytes are passed through `msgpack.unpackb()`, and if the result is a dict, it is passed to `deserialize_type()` with a safe minimal `cls_map`. This exercises the real-world attack surface of the serialization layer.

4. **`_fuzz_deserialize_type_tensor_path`** (target 3) -- Specifically targets the Tensor deserialization path in `deserialize_type()` from `/app/minisgl/python/minisgl/message/utils.py`. It crafts dicts with `"__type__": "Tensor"` and varies the `dtype` string (sometimes valid numpy dtypes, sometimes fuzzed strings) and buffer bytes. This exercises `getattr(np, dtype_str)` and `np.frombuffer()` with potentially mismatched buffer/dtype combinations.

5. **`_fuzz_deserialize_any_crafted`** (target 4) -- Tests `_deserialize_any()` with recursively constructed fuzz data structures (nested dicts, lists, tuples with `__type__` keys). Uses a helper function `_build_fuzz_data()` with depth limiting (max depth 5) to prevent stack overflow. Tests all code paths: dict with `__type__` (triggers `deserialize_type`), dict without `__type__` (recursive dict processing), lists, tuples, and primitives.

6. **`_fuzz_deserialize_type_safe_cls`** (target 5) -- Tests the object instantiation path (`cls(**kwargs)`) by using a safe `_FuzzSafeClass` dataclass in the `cls_map`. Sometimes adds unexpected extra keyword arguments to test error handling when constructing objects with wrong arguments.

### Key Design Decisions

- **No GPU required:** All targets are pure Python or CPU-only numpy/torch operations.
- **Safe cls_map:** Uses a trivial `_FuzzSafeClass` dataclass instead of real minisgl classes to avoid uncontrolled object instantiation while still testing the deserialization logic.
- **Pre-imported heavy dependencies:** torch, numpy, msgpack, zmq, and transformers are imported before `atheris.instrument_imports()` to avoid instrumenting their code (which would slow startup by minutes). Only minisgl modules are instrumented for coverage guidance.
- **Acceptable exceptions** are caught silently: `ValueError`, `TypeError`, `KeyError`, `IndexError`, `AssertionError`, `UnicodeDecodeError`, `struct.error`, `msgpack.exceptions.UnpackException`, `OverflowError`, `AttributeError`, `RecursionError`.
- **Suspicious exceptions propagate:** `MemoryError`, `SystemError`, segfaults, and other unexpected errors will cause the fuzzer to report a crash.

### Verification

The fuzzer was tested successfully, completing **271,249 iterations in 11 seconds** with no crashes found. It discovered coverage across 49 edges and 115 features, and automatically identified useful dictionary entries including `"Tensor"` (for the tensor deserialization path).</result>

import atheris
import sys
import tokenize

# Import heavy transitive dependencies BEFORE atheris.instrument_imports()
# to avoid instrumenting hundreds of unrelated modules (traitlets, prompt_toolkit,
# pygments, jedi, parso, etc.) which causes very slow startup.
import traitlets  # noqa: F401
import pygments  # noqa: F401
import jedi  # noqa: F401
import parso  # noqa: F401
import prompt_toolkit  # noqa: F401
import IPython.core.interactiveshell  # noqa: F401 - pulls in most of IPython

# Only instrument the specific modules we are fuzzing
with atheris.instrument_imports():
    from IPython.core.inputtransformer2 import TransformerManager
    from IPython.core.splitinput import split_user_input
    from IPython.utils.tokenutil import token_at_cursor

tm = TransformerManager()


def TestOneInput(data):
    fdp = atheris.FuzzedDataProvider(data)
    fuzz_string = fdp.ConsumeUnicodeNoSurrogates(fdp.ConsumeIntInRange(0, 4096))
    cursor_pos = fdp.ConsumeIntInRange(0, len(fuzz_string))

    try:
        tm.transform_cell(fuzz_string)
    except (SyntaxError, ValueError, TypeError, tokenize.TokenError, IndentationError):
        pass

    try:
        tm.check_complete(fuzz_string)
    except (SyntaxError, ValueError, TypeError, tokenize.TokenError, IndentationError):
        pass

    try:
        split_user_input(fuzz_string)
    except (SyntaxError, ValueError, TypeError, tokenize.TokenError, IndentationError):
        pass

    try:
        token_at_cursor(fuzz_string, cursor_pos)
    except (SyntaxError, ValueError, TypeError, tokenize.TokenError, IndentationError):
        pass


def main():
    atheris.Setup(sys.argv, TestOneInput)
    atheris.Fuzz()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
